title: 3-Read Friday #64: Checking Understanding, SEND, and Interleaving
author: Craig Barton
summary: Issue #64 of 3-Read Friday opens with David Didau's argument that teachers often avoid rigorously checking for understanding because discovering a lack of it is uncomfortable to confront -- a point Barton flags as controversial but true. Matthew Evans then opens a planned trilogy on SEND (special educational needs and disabilities) provision, framing it as a 'wicked problem' using Rittel and Webber's theory, with Norwich's 'dilemma of difference' as the organizing tension. Blake Harvard closes the issue summarizing a study that isolates interleaving's effect from spacing effects, finding students perform worse on interleaved quizzes in the short term but significantly better on delayed tests. Barton frames all three as evidence-grounded challenges to comfortable classroom defaults -- taking the easy answer over the hard truth, avoiding a genuinely difficult policy debate, and sticking with the more popular but less effective blocked-practice format.
points: Didau's diagnosis reframes weak checks for understanding as motivated avoidance, not a skills gap: teachers who call on eager volunteers are often protecting themselves from the discomfort of discovering students don't understand.

Evans's SEND framing borrows 'wicked problems' theory to argue that quick, tame-sounding fixes to the SEND crisis are likely to backfire because they misjudge the depth and self-reinforcing nature of the underlying tensions.

Harvard's summarized study isolates interleaving from spacing (most prior interleaving research confounds the two), finding interleaved practice underperforms on immediate quizzes but outperforms blocked practice on every category of question a month later.

Barton's synthesis: each piece asks teachers to tolerate short-term discomfort (revealed ignorance, unresolved policy tension, worse-looking quiz scores) in exchange for a more accurate or durable long-term outcome.
quotes: I think one of the reasons some teachers do not effectively check for understanding—so they ask the high-attaining, confident volunteers with their hands eagerly raised instead of asking everyone to put their answer on a mini-whiteboard—is that they would rather not know a lack of understanding exists because it is difficult to deal with.

I don't know enough about SEND. It's as simple as that. Matthew's recent trilogy of posts - the first of which is linked to here - has helped me better appreciate the crisis we are in, and potential ways out of it.
Blake has found an interleaving study with a super simple classroom application. Enjoy!
